mainTopic: Facts about animal reproduction in a ברייתא: birth versus eggs, timing of birth, mating styles, pregnancy lengths, and the snake's seven years
overview: This amud continues a ברייתא full of facts about how creatures reproduce. It says the דולפנין reproduce like people. It then gives a sign for whether a species gives birth or lays eggs, and the גמרא corrects that sign from the testicles to the male organ itself, because of the case of the wild goose. Next the ברייתא says each species gives birth at the time of day it mates. The גמרא shows why this matters: since chickens lay only by day, an egg found before daybreak on יום טוב is permitted, and רבי יוחנן's ruling about an egg that mostly came out and went back in explains the case. The ברייתא teaches that species with the same mating style and pregnancy length can breed together. Most animals mate face-to-back, but fish, humans and the snake mate face-to-face, because the שכינה spoke with them, and the camel mates back-to-back. A long list then matches each animal's pregnancy length to a tree that ripens in the same time, ending with the snake's seven years. The גמרא derives the seven years from the snake's curse using a one-to-seven ratio, then challenges it with a one-to-three ratio that would give nine years. The answer to that challenge comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Dolphins reproduce like humans
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states that דולפנין reproduce the way people do.
steps.simpleTranslation: The דולפנין reproduce and multiply like people.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells us one more fact about reproduction: the דולפנין reproduce like human beings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is listing creatures and how they reproduce. 'Like people' means the female carries the young inside her and gives birth to live offspring, not eggs. רש"י has a different text, 'מבני אדם' (from people): if a man has relations with them, they conceive from him.

keyTerms.meaning: Sea creatures (often identified as dolphins) that reproduce like humans

phrases.english: The dulfanin reproduce and multiply like people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from the previous section of the daf about which creatures give birth and which lay eggs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דולפנין reproduce like humans and give birth to live young.

steps.title: What are דולפנין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what creature the word דולפנין refers to, and רב יהודה answers: 'sons of the sea'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are דולפנין? רב יהודה said: Sons of the sea.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what this unusual word means. רב יהודה explains that דולפנין are 'בני ימא', sea creatures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a word-definition question, not a challenge. Nobody is attacking the ברייתא. רב יהודה identifies the creature as a sea-dweller so we know what the ברייתא is talking about. Some explain 'sons of the sea' as creatures thought to be half human and half fish.

keyTerms.meaning: What is? (a request for a definition)
An אמורא who explains the term

phrases.english: What are dulfanin?
Rav Yehuda said: Sons of the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the unfamiliar term from the ברייתא in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which creature is meant by דולפנין.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב יהודה: they are 'sons of the sea', sea creatures.

steps.title: The sign for live birth versus eggs
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives a rule: a male with external testicles means the species gives birth, and internal testicles means it lays eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any creature whose testicles are on the outside gives birth, and any whose testicles are on the inside lays eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a general sign for telling whether a species gives birth to live young or lays eggs. It sets up the rule that the גמרא will soon test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sign is a physical feature of the male: where his testicles are located. If they are external, the female of that species gives birth to live young. If they are internal, the female lays eggs.
steps.confusionAlert: The word בֵּיצָיו here means the male's testicles, not eggs. The words מטיל ביצים, 'lays eggs', are about the female of the species.

phrases.english: Any whose testicles are on the outside gives birth,
and any whose are on the inside lays eggs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The ברייתא continues with a general rule about reproduction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: External testicles mean the species gives birth. Internal testicles mean it lays eggs.

steps.title: Challenge from the domestic and wild goose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rule. According to אביי, the wild goose has external testicles, yet both kinds of goose lay eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But שמואל said: a goose and a wild goose are diverse kinds with each other. And we asked about it: what is the reason? אביי said: this one's testicles are outside, and this one's are inside. Yet both lay eggs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא's rule with a counter-example. It brings שמואל's ruling about two kinds of geese and אביי's explanation of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל says a domestic goose and a wild goose count as כלאים (forbidden mixed kinds). אביי explains why they are different species: one has external testicles and the other has internal testicles. But both kinds of geese lay eggs. So external testicles cannot be a sign of live birth, which contradicts the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it / asked about it

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Shmuel say:

phrases.aramaic: אֲוָוז וַאֲוָוז בָּר כִּלְאַיִם זֶה בָּזֶה,
phrases.english: a goose and a wild goose are diverse kinds with each other,
and we discussed it: what is the reason?
Abaye said: this one's testicles are outside,
and this one's testicles are inside,
and both of them lay eggs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא's rule from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that external testicles mean live birth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wild goose has external testicles according to אביי, yet it lays eggs. So the sign fails.

steps.title: The sign is the male organ, not the testicles
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: the sign is whether the male reproductive organ is external or internal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: any creature whose male organ is on the outside gives birth, and any whose male organ is on the inside lays eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reinterpreting the ברייתא's sign. It refers to the male organ, not the testicles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule now depends on where the male reproductive organ is, not where the testicles are. The wild goose has external testicles, but its organ is internal. So it fits the rule that it lays eggs, and אביי's distinction between the two geese still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The final sign: if the male reproductive organ is external, the species gives birth. If it is internal, the species lays eggs. The location of the testicles is not the sign.

phrases.english: Rather, any whose male organ is on the outside gives birth,
on the inside lays eggs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 4 by reinterpreting the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sign was thought to be the location of the testicles.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sign is the location of the male reproductive organ, so the wild goose (external testicles, internal organ) lays eggs as expected.

steps.title: Animals give birth at the time of day they mate
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: a species that mates by day gives birth by day, one that mates by night gives birth by night, and one that mates at both times gives birth at both times.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any species that mates during the day gives birth during the day. One that mates at night gives birth at night. Any species that mates both by day and by night gives birth both by day and by night.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא about how animals reproduce continues with a new rule. Birth time follows mating time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the ברייתא gave a sign for whether a species gives birth or lays eggs. Now it adds a second fact about nature: the time of day of birth matches the time of day of mating. This sets up the next lines, which name the animals and then show a practical use for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives birth (here, for a bird, also lays eggs)

phrases.english: Any species whose mating is by day gives birth by day;
one whose mating is at night gives birth at night;

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁתַּשְׁמִישׁוֹ בֵּין בַּיּוֹם בֵּין בַּלַּיְלָה —
phrases.english: any species whose mating is both by day and at night
gives birth both by day and at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא about animal reproduction with a new rule about timing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Time of birth matches time of mating: day, night, or both.

steps.title: Naming the animals: chicken, bat, and human
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא identifies the animals: a chicken mates and lays by day, a bat mates and gives birth at night, and a human (and similar creatures) does both at any time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Mates by day and gives birth by day: this is the chicken. Mates at night and gives birth at night: this is the bat. Mates both by day and at night and gives birth at both times: this is a human and anything similar to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a concrete example for each part of the ברייתא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke in general terms. The גמרא now attaches a real animal to each category. The chicken example is the key one, because the next steps build a halacha on the fact that chickens lay only by day.

keyTerms.meaning: And everything that is like it

phrases.english: Mates by day, gives birth by day: a chicken;
at night, gives birth at night: a bat;
mates both by day and at night
and gives birth both by day and at night:
a human and anything similar to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains which animals belong to each category in the ברייתא's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Chicken = day only; bat = night only; human = both.

steps.title: What practical difference does this make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what halachic difference it makes whether an animal gives birth by day or by night.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the practical difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why this nature fact matters for halacha. This short question sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase למאי נפקא מינה means: what practical outcome depends on this? It is not an attack on the ברייתא. It is a request to see where the rule is actually used.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: For what is there a practical difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical use of the rule just explained.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A halachic case that depends on knowing when an animal gives birth or lays eggs.

steps.title: An egg found early on יום טוב morning is permitted
steps.stepSummary: The answer comes from רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא: if someone checked a chicken's nest on ערב יום טוב and found nothing, then rose early on יום טוב and found an egg, the egg may be eaten. We assume he did not check carefully.
steps.simpleTranslation: It matters for the ruling of רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא. He said: if someone checked a chicken's nest on ערב יום טוב and found no egg, and the next morning he rose early and found an egg, it may be eaten on יום טוב. We say: he did not check well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a case about an egg found on יום טוב. Because chickens lay only by day, an egg found before daybreak was not laid that night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An egg laid on יום טוב itself is forbidden to eat that day (see מסכת ביצה). The man found the egg very early, before daylight, while it was still night. Since chickens lay only by day, the egg must have been laid on ערב יום טוב, so we say he simply missed it when he checked.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say / we can assume

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the egg is permitted because it was found in the morning. It is permitted because it was found before daylight, during the night, when a chicken does not lay. So it must have come from before יום טוב.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a fact from nature (chickens lay only by day) decides a real halachic question about eating on יום טוב.

phrases.english: For the ruling of Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: as Rav Mari, son of Rav Kahana, said:

phrases.aramaic: בָּדַק בְּקִינָּה שֶׁל תַּרְנְגוֹלִין מֵעֶרֶב יוֹם טוֹב
phrases.english: If one checked a chickens' nest on the eve of the festival
and did not find an egg in it,
and the next day he rose early and found an egg in it,
it is permitted to be eaten on the festival;
we say: he did not check carefully.
phrases.notes: Since a chicken does not lay at night, the egg must have already been there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8 by showing a halacha that depends on the chicken laying only by day.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An egg found before daybreak on יום טוב is permitted, since chickens do not lay at night; it must have been laid on ערב יום טוב and missed.

steps.title: But he did check carefully
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the case says he checked the nest, so how can we assume he did not check well?
steps.simpleTranslation: But he did check carefully!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation that the man just missed the egg. This sets up the next step, which gives a better explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling describes a real check that found nothing. Saying 'he did not check well' seems to ignore that detail. So the question is: if the egg truly was not there on ערב יום טוב, how can it be permitted?

phrases.english: But he did check carefully!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation 'he did not check well' given in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that the owner missed the egg when checking.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case states that he checked, so we should accept that the egg was truly not in the nest on ערב יום טוב.

steps.title: The egg came mostly out and went back in, following רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the egg mostly came out of the hen on ערב יום טוב and then went back in. Following רבי יוחנן, such an egg counts as already laid before יום טוב, so it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that most of the egg came out and then went back in. This follows רבי יוחנן, who said: an egg that mostly came out on ערב יום טוב and then went back in is permitted to be eaten on יום טוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts that he checked well and gives a new reason the egg is permitted. It relies on a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even with a careful check, the egg could have been hidden inside the hen at that time. Once most of the egg came out on ערב יום טוב, halacha treats it as already laid then, even though it slipped back in. So when it fully came out at night, it is not a new egg of יום טוב, and it may be eaten.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא whose ruling supports this answer

steps.whatToRemember: Chickens lay only by day. So an egg found before daybreak on יום טוב is permitted. Even if the nest was checked well, the egg may have mostly come out on ערב יום טוב and gone back in, and רבי יוחנן rules such an egg counts as already laid.

phrases.english: Say: it was a case where most of it came out and went back in,
and this follows Rabbi Yoḥanan,
as Rabbi Yoḥanan said:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּיצָה שֶׁיָּצְתָה רוּבָּהּ מֵעֶרֶב יוֹם טוֹב וְחוֹזֶרֶת —
phrases.english: An egg most of which came out on the festival eve and then went back in
is permitted to be eaten on the festival.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 by redefining the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא) supported by an earlier ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since he checked well, the egg was not there and should be forbidden as laid on יום טוב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The egg mostly came out on ערב יום טוב and went back in; per רבי יוחנן it counts as laid before יום טוב and is permitted.

steps.title: Same mating and same pregnancy length allow cross-breeding
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. Animals of different species can produce young together, and nurse each other's young, if they share the same way of mating and the same length of pregnancy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any animals whose mating and pregnancy are the same can give birth from each other and raise each other's young.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a general rule for when two different species can produce offspring together and nurse each other's young.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things must match: the way the animals mate (תשמיש) and how long the pregnancy lasts (עיבור). If both match, the species can produce young together and can nurse each other's young. The rest of the ברייתא fills in the details of these two things, first mating and then pregnancy length.

keyTerms.meaning: Pregnancy, the time of carrying the young

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule helps explain how a strange-looking newborn could have come from a different species. That question matters for the laws of בכור discussed in this פרק.

phrases.english: Any [species] whose mating and pregnancy are the same
can give birth from one another and raise [nurse] one another's young.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא last quoted in Step 6, after the גמרא's side-discussion of the egg on יום טוב (steps 8–11), and continues its list of facts about animal nature.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Species that share the same mating style and pregnancy length can produce offspring together and nurse each other's young.

steps.title: Most animals mate face-to-back, except three
steps.stepSummary: All creatures mate face-to-back except fish, humans and the snake, which mate face-to-face.
steps.simpleTranslation: All creatures mate with face toward the back of the neck, except three that mate face-to-face: fish, humans and the snake.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the first part of the rule, the way of mating, and lists three exceptions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual way is that the male comes from behind the female (פנים כנגד עורף). Three creatures are exceptions and mate face-to-face. This list sets up the גמרא's question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Face toward the back of the neck (from behind)

phrases.english: All [creatures] mate face toward the back of the neck,
except for three that mate
face-to-face,
and these are they: fish, and man, and snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the 'mating' part (תשמיש) of the rule in Step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Face-to-back is the norm. Fish, humans and the snake are the exceptions and mate face-to-face.

steps.title: Why are these three creatures different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what makes fish, humans and the snake different from all other creatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about these three?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the exception. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the ברייתא. It is a request to understand why these three particular creatures, which seem to have nothing in common, share this unusual trait.

phrases.english: And what is different about these three?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the exception listed in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do fish, humans and the snake have in common that makes them mate face-to-face?

steps.title: Because the שכינה spoke with them
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports the answer given in ארץ ישראל: these three are different because the שכינה spoke with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came [from ארץ ישראל], he said that in the West they say: since the שכינה spoke with them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי brings the explanation from the חכמים of ארץ ישראל: these three creatures had God speak with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: God spoke to the fish that swallowed יונה, to humans such as אדם and the נביאים, and to the snake after the sin in גן עדן. Being spoken to face-to-face by the שכינה is reflected in their face-to-face nature.

keyTerms.meaning: When [he] came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
An אמורא who brought teachings from ארץ ישראל to בבל
In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.confusionAlert: 'מערבא' (the West) does not mean a western country. It is the Babylonian name for ארץ ישראל, which lies west of בבל.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came [from Eretz Yisrael],
[he said:] they say in the West:
Since the Divine Presence spoke with them.
phrases.notes: The fish (יונה), man (אדם and the נביאים), the snake (בראשית ג׳).

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמְרִי בְּמַעְרְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The three are different because the שכינה spoke with each of them.

steps.title: The camel mates back-to-back
steps.stepSummary: A תנא adds one more unusual case: the camel mates back-to-back.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: a camel [mates] back to back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a short teaching about one more animal with an unusual mating position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far there were two styles: face-to-back (most animals) and face-to-face (the three exceptions). This teaching adds a third style that only the camel has.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא taught (introduces a ברייתא teaching)

phrases.english: A tanna taught: A camel [mates] back to back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further exception to the list of mating positions in Step 13.

steps.title: Pregnancy lengths of animals matched to trees
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists how long several animals carry their young and matches each one to a tree or plant that takes the same time to ripen.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A chicken takes 21 days, and its match among trees is the almond. A dog takes 50 days, and its match is the fig. A cat takes 52 days, and its match is the mulberry. A pig takes 60 days, and its match is the apple. A fox and all kinds of שרצים take six months, and their match is grain.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא now covers the second part of the Step 12 rule, the length of pregnancy, by giving a list of animals and their times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each animal's time (for the chicken, until the egg hatches) is matched to a plant that needs the same time from flowering to ripening. This list tells us which animals share the same pregnancy length, which is one of the two conditions in Step 12.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא explained both parts of the rule. Mating: most animals face-to-back, fish, humans and the snake face-to-face, and the camel back-to-back. Pregnancy: each animal has a set length, and each length is matched to a plant.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A chicken: after twenty-one days,
and its match among trees is the almond,
a dog: after fifty days,
and its match among trees is the fig,
a cat: after fifty-two days,
and its match among trees is the mulberry,
a pig: after sixty days,
its match among trees is the apple,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוּעָל וְכׇל מִינֵי שְׁרָצִים — שִׁשָּׁה חֳדָשִׁים,
phrases.english: a fox and all kinds of creeping animals: six months,
and their match among trees [plants] is grain.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: תַּרְנְגוֹלֶת — לְעֶשְׂרִים וְאֶחָד יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from mating positions to the second part of the Step 12 rule, the length of pregnancy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Chicken 21 days (almond), dog 50 (fig), cat 52 (mulberry), pig 60 (apple), fox and שרצים six months (grain).

steps.title: Livestock and wild animals matched to trees
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues its list. Small kosher animals take 5 months (like the vine). Large non-kosher animals take 12 months (like the date palm). Large kosher animals take 9 months (like the olive). Several wild animals take 3 years (like the white fig).
steps.simpleTranslation: Small kosher animals give birth after five months, and the matching tree is the grapevine. Large non-kosher animals give birth after twelve months, and the matching tree is the date palm. Large kosher animals give birth after nine months, and the matching tree is the olive. The wolf, lion, bear, leopard, ברדלס, elephant, monkey and long-tailed ape give birth after three years, and the matching tree is the white fig.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going with its list. It gives more animals' pregnancy lengths and pairs each with a tree that ripens in the same time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every line follows the same pattern: an animal group, then its pregnancy length, then 'וכנגדן באילן' plus a tree. Pay attention to the categories. Small versus large and kosher versus non-kosher each change the number. A large kosher animal like a cow takes 9 months, but a large non-kosher animal like a donkey takes 12.

keyTerms.meaning: A wild predator, often identified as a hyena or a kind of leopard
White figs, a slow-ripening kind of fig

steps.confusionAlert: The line 'טהורה לתשעה חדשים' does not say which kind of animal it means. It continues from the line before it, so it means large kosher livestock, like a cow.

phrases.english: Small kosher livestock give birth after five months,
and the matching tree is the grapevine.

phrases.aramaic: בְּהֵמָה גַּסָּה טְמֵאָה — לִשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חוֹדֶשׁ,
phrases.english: Large non-kosher livestock give birth after twelve months,
and the matching tree is the date palm.
Large kosher livestock give birth after nine months,
phrases.notes: 'Large' is carried over from the line before.

phrases.english: and the matching tree is the olive.
The wolf, the lion, the bear, and the leopard,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַבַּרְדְּלָס וְהַפִּיל וְהַקּוֹף וְהַקִּיפוֹף — לְשָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים,
phrases.english: and the bardelas, the elephant, the monkey, and the long-tailed ape give birth after three years,
and the matching tree is the white fig.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא begun in step 17
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small kosher animals take 5 months (vine), large non-kosher 12 months (date palm), large kosher 9 months (olive), and large wild animals 3 years (white fig).

steps.title: The viper takes seventy years, like the carob
steps.stepSummary: The אפעה (viper) carries its young for seventy years. Its matching tree is the carob, which takes seventy years from planting until its fruit is fully ripe.
steps.simpleTranslation: A viper gives birth after seventy years, and the matching tree is the carob. This carob takes seventy years from the time it is planted until its fruit is fully ripe. Its own 'pregnancy' stage is three years.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the most extreme pairing so far: the viper and the carob tree, both seventy years. It then explains why the carob fits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Seventy years sounds strange, so the ברייתא shows that the carob really does take that long to fully produce fruit. It also says the carob has a three-year 'עיבור' (pregnancy-like) stage. The exact meaning of that phrase is discussed by the commentators.

keyTerms.meaning: The full ripening of its fruit

phrases.english: A viper gives birth after seventy years,
and the matching tree is the carob.
This carob, from the time it is planted

phrases.aramaic: עַד שְׁעַת גְּמַר פֵּירוֹתָיו — שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה,
phrases.english: until its fruit is fully ripe, takes seventy years,
and its 'pregnancy' period is three years.
phrases.notes: The commentators explain this phrase in different ways.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same ברייתא list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The viper takes seventy years, matching the carob's seventy years to full fruit.

steps.title: The snake takes seven years and has no matching tree
steps.stepSummary: The נחש (snake) carries its young for seven years. The ברייתא says no tree matches 'that wicked one.' A second opinion (יש אומרים) says the מוכססים do match.
steps.simpleTranslation: A snake gives birth after seven years, and for that wicked creature we have found no partner among the trees. Some say the מוכססים match it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends its list with the snake. The first opinion says no tree matches the snake. Another opinion names a plant that does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling the snake 'that wicked one' points back to the snake in גן עדן. This sets up the next question: where do we know the snake's seven years from? The יש אומרים holds that a plant called מוכססים also takes seven years, so the snake does have a match.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That wicked one', the snake of גן עדן
A plant said to take seven years to ripen

phrases.english: A snake gives birth after seven years,
and for that wicked one we have found no partner.
And some say: the mukhsasim are its match.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final item of the ברייתא list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The snake takes seven years. The first opinion says no tree matches it, and the יש אומרים says the מוכססים do.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא pairs each animal's pregnancy with a tree's ripening time. It ends with the snake: seven years and, in the first opinion, no matching tree.

steps.title: Where do we know the snake's seven years from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the snake carries its young for seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these words?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source. This short question sets up the next move, where a verse will be brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most of the numbers in the list could be known just by watching animals. The snake's seven years, however, is tied to its curse, so the גמרא looks for a verse that teaches it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these words? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these words derived?
phrases.notes: Refers to the snake's seven years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the last item in the list
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the snake's seven-year pregnancy

steps.title: The source is the curse of the snake
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב (and some say רבי יהושע בן חנניה) brings the verse 'Cursed are you more than all the animals and all the beasts of the field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב, and some trace it to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: as it says, 'Cursed are you from among all the domesticated animals and from among all the beasts of the field.'
steps.whatsHappening: An answer is given: the source is the curse the snake received in גן עדן. The snake was cursed more than all other animals, which here means its pregnancy is longer than all of theirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being 'cursed more than all animals' is read as being given a longer pregnancy than any of them. The verse names two groups, בהמה (domesticated animals) and חית השדה (wild animals). The next step questions why both are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: And some trace it to (a different teacher)
Beasts of the field, meaning wild animals

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָטוּ בָּהּ מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָא,
phrases.english: and some trace it to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya:
as it says: 'Cursed are you from among all the domesticated animals'
'and from among all the beasts of the field' (Genesis 3:14).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The snake's curse 'more than all the animals' teaches that its pregnancy is longer than theirs.

steps.title: Why does the verse also mention wild animals?
steps.stepSummary: If the snake is cursed more than domesticated animals, it is surely cursed more than wild animals, so the second phrase seems extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was cursed more than the domesticated animals, then surely it was cursed more than the wild animals!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה, continuing his own derivation, points out that part of the verse seems unnecessary. This sets up a new teaching from the extra words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shortest pregnancy among domesticated animals (a goat, 5 months) is longer than the shortest among wild animals (a cat, about 52 days). So being cursed beyond the domesticated animals should already mean being cursed beyond the wild animals. That makes 'ומכל חית השדה' look extra, and the next step will explain what it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not all the more so?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question against רב יהודה's answer. It is a question on the wording of the verse, and its answer becomes the actual source for the number seven.

phrases.english: If it was cursed more than the domesticated animals,
then surely more than the wild animals?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם מִבְּהֵמָה נִתְקַלְּלָה, מֵחַיָּה לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the verse just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'ומכל חית השדה' in the verse
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Through a כל שכן argument, the phrase about wild animals seems extra, since being cursed more than domesticated animals already covers it.

steps.title: The one-to-seven ratio gives seven years
steps.stepSummary: The extra phrase teaches a ratio. A donkey's pregnancy (12 months) is about seven times a cat's (52 days). In the same way, the snake's pregnancy is seven times a donkey's, which is seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the verse comes to tell you: just as the domesticated animal was cursed more than the wild animal, one to seven (which case is that? the donkey compared to the cat), so too the snake was cursed more than the domesticated animal, one to seven. That comes to seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה, completing his derivation, explains that the extra words teach a comparison. The gap between domesticated and wild animals is the same gap between the snake and domesticated animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cat carries for about 52 days, and 52 × 7 = 364, about one year, which is a donkey's pregnancy. So a בהמה is 'cursed' seven times more than a חיה. The snake's pregnancy is then seven times the donkey's one year: seven years, just as the ברייתא said.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, it comes to tell you
A donkey compared to a cat

steps.whatToRemember: The extra words 'ומכל חית השדה' teach a 1:7 ratio. Cat (about 52 days) × 7 = donkey (1 year), and donkey (1 year) × 7 = snake (7 years).
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic way the גמרא learns from words that seem extra in a verse: the 'extra' phrase is turned into a precise new teaching.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to tell you:
just as the domesticated animal was cursed more than the wild animal,
by a ratio of one to seven,
and what case is that? A donkey compared to a cat,
phrases.notes: A short side-question and answer: 12 months versus about 52 days.

phrases.english: so too it (the snake) was cursed more than the domesticated animal,

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת לְשֶׁבַע, דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ שַׁב שְׁנֵי.
phrases.english: by one to seven, which comes to seven years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question about the extra phrase and completes the source for seven years
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the extra phrase as teaching a ratio
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase about wild animals seemed to add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: It teaches the 1:7 ratio, which gives the snake seven years (seven times a donkey's one year).

steps.title: Maybe the curse uses a one-to-three ratio instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes a different reading of the verse: the חיה was cursed beyond the בהמה by a one-to-three ratio.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: just as the wild animals were cursed more than the domesticated animals by a ratio of one year to three years...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge to the answer it just gave. It suggests a different ratio could be the one the verse hints at. This step only sets up the challenge; the full point comes in step 28.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 built its answer on a seven-to-one ratio, the cat compared with the donkey. Here the גמרא says the verse's two groups, בהמה and חיה, could point to a different ratio: one to three. If that is the right ratio, the math for the snake will come out differently.

keyTerms.meaning: Say (instead): a word that introduces an alternative reading, often as a challenge
Just as: sets up a comparison

phrases.english: Say: just as the wild animal was cursed more than the domesticated animal,
phrases.notes: אימא signals the גמרא is offering a competing interpretation.

phrases.english: by a ratio of one year to three years,
phrases.notes: A one-to-three ratio, not the one-to-seven ratio used before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to the ratio-based answer given in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The seven-to-one ratio (cat to donkey) used in step 24 to derive seven years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse's comparison of חיה and בהמה could just as well point to the one-to-three ratio between a lion and a donkey.

steps.title: Which animals show the one-to-three ratio?
steps.stepSummary: Inside its challenge, the גמרא pauses to ask which animals actually show this one-to-three ratio.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what case is that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops briefly in the middle of its challenge to ask for a concrete example of the one-to-three ratio. This is a short clarifying question that sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ratio only proves something if real animals actually show it. So the גמרא asks which wild animal is three times slower than which domesticated animal.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is it? A request to identify the specific case

phrases.english: And what is that?
phrases.notes: An interjection asking for the specific animals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the concrete example behind the one-to-three ratio claimed in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which wild animal and which domesticated animal show a one-to-three pregnancy ratio.

steps.title: The lion compared with the donkey
steps.stepSummary: The example is the ארי (three-year pregnancy) compared with the חמור (one-year pregnancy).
steps.simpleTranslation: A lion compared with a donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the example: the lion, a חיה, compared with the donkey, a בהמה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The donkey carries its young for one year, and the lion carries for three years. So the wild animal is three times slower than the domesticated animal, which is exactly the one-to-three ratio.

keyTerms.meaning: Lion (a wild animal; carries for three years)
Donkey (a domesticated animal; carries for one year)

steps.confusionAlert: The donkey is the same animal used in step 24. There it was compared with the cat (seven to one). Here it is compared with the lion (one to three). The same donkey anchors two different ratios, and that is the whole problem.

phrases.english: A lion compared with a donkey,
phrases.notes: Lion: three years; donkey: one year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the interjected question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lion (three years) compared with the donkey (one year) shows the one-to-three ratio.

steps.title: Then the snake should carry for nine years
steps.stepSummary: Applying the one-to-three ratio to the snake gives nine years, not seven, which contradicts the earlier answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, the snake was cursed more than the wild animal by a ratio of one year to three years, which comes out to nine years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge. If the snake is cursed beyond the wild animals by the same one-to-three ratio, its pregnancy would be nine years, not seven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lion carries for three years. Three times that is nine years. So the verse could just as easily teach nine years for the נחש, and the challenge is: why did step 24 pick the seven-to-one ratio that gives seven years?
steps.whatToRemember: The challenge: if you use the lion-to-donkey ratio (one to three), the snake's pregnancy comes out to nine years instead of seven. The גמרא must now explain why the seven-year reading is correct.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a ratio drawn from a verse needs a reason for choosing one pair of animals over another. Otherwise different pairs give different answers.

phrases.english: so too, it [the snake] was cursed more than the wild animal
phrases.notes: The 'wild animal' here means the lion.

phrases.english: by a ratio of one year to three years,
phrases.notes: The same ratio applied a second time.

phrases.english: which comes out to nine years.
phrases.notes: Three years (the lion) times three equals nine.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּךְ נִתְקַלֵּל הוּא מֵחַיָּה אַחַת לְשָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge that began in step 25, now using the example from step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion in step 24 that the snake carries for seven years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Applying the lion-to-donkey ratio (one to three) to the snake gives nine years, so the verse does not clearly prove seven years.
